open-question.question: Should docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md gain a chain that starts from an empty repository with the bootstrap line, now that the bootstrap commits and a headless chain can include it without leaving files behind, or do the chains keep assuming an already-bootstrapped repository?
open-question.recommendation: A short section before "Starting a milestone" that runs the bootstrap line and a define-milestone-goal line from a fresh repository, naming git init and /init as prose preconditions, is what makes the milestone's point visible on the one page about unattended runs, giving an end-to-end path that a bootstrap-only section would not; the extra placeholder costs one legend line, and the chain's clean-tree claim holds because the bootstrap commits the /init-written CLAUDE.md with its own edit.
open-question.alternative: Add a new section to docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, placed before "Starting a milestone", that runs from a fresh git repository through the bootstrap line and `define-milestone-goal "<goal>"`, and hands off to the existing "Starting a milestone" chain. The prose would name `git init` and `/init` as preconditions instead of putting them in the fenced block. It covers the whole headless lifecycle, from an empty repository to a finished milestone, and it shows the milestone's point: with the exemption gone, every documented chain leaves a clean tree. That makes design claim 12's clean-tree promise visible in the one page about unattended runs. It adds a new placeholder, `<goal>`, to a page whose legend defines only `<milestone_id>` and `<project-root>`, so the notation section grows too. The steps that come before the bootstrap (git init, and /init writing CLAUDE.md) cannot be `/cairn:<skill>` lines under the page's "every line is a complete invocation" rule. And if /init leaves an uncommitted CLAUDE.md, the chain's clean-tree claim holds only if the pre-existing dirty-paths question is settled so the bootstrap handles that file safely.

Add a short section, "Bootstrapping a project", whose fenced block holds just the one `claude -p "/cairn:init-milestone-base-workflow"` line, like the one-line "Finishing a milestone" section. Its sentences say to run it once in a git repository after /init, and that it leaves its scaffold committed. It documents the only skill a headless run could call that no chain covers, without adding a placeholder or breaking the page's line rule. It follows a pattern the page already uses (a one-line section), so the added text stays small and cannot go stale on define-milestone-goal's argument. It is not really a chain, so the page still gives no end-to-end path from an empty repository. A reader who wants to go on to a first milestone has to write the define-milestone-goal step themselves. Documenting a run that happens once per project arguably gains little over the README's existing setup instructions.

Put the bootstrap line at the top of the existing "Starting a milestone" chain. The skill is idempotent and stops without changes on an already-bootstrapped project, so the same chain would work on the first milestone and on every later one. No new section. One chain then works whether or not the repository has been bootstrapped, and the run cannot fail later because the scaffold is missing. It does not help an empty repository by itself: the chain's goto-next-milestone line still needs a milestone already defined, and that has to come after the bootstrap. So the chain's own precondition ("a milestone is defined and the pointer reads none") contradicts the bootstrap line in front of it. It also adds a headless model run, with its prerequisite checks, to every milestone start just to reach a no-op on every run after the first. Whether that no-op run prints a distinct line depends on how the reporting-shape question is settled.

Leave docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md without a bootstrap chain: every chain keeps assuming a bootstrapped repository, and at most one sentence in the page's opening paragraph notes that the bootstrap runs once beforehand. The milestone's scope stays at the three places the goal names. It avoids documenting a step that happens once and is usually interactive (it usually follows /init and a conversational discuss-milestone-goal) on a page meant for repeatable unattended runs. It also leaves nothing on the page that depends on how the sibling questions about subject, reporting, and dirty paths are settled. It passes up the change the goal is about: once the bootstrap commits, it is safe in a headless chain, and the page would still not say so. A reader could reasonably assume from the old exemption that the bootstrap has to stay manual. The page's claim that "every skill commits what it changes" also stays untested for the one skill that only now meets it.

open-question.question: Does the git prerequisite pass whenever the workspace root is inside any git work tree (for example a subdirectory of a larger repository), or only when the workspace root is itself the repository's top level, and does a freshly initialized repository with no commits yet pass?
open-question.recommendation: One `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` probe asks for exactly what the shared commit procedure needs, which works from a subdirectory and on an unborn HEAD, so monorepo subprojects and brand-new repositories pass and a plain "git init, then re-run" remedy is sufficient; top-level-only refuses correct subprojects and invites a nested git init, commit-required enforces nothing the procedure needs, and a nested-repository advisory lands after the commit has already gone where the enclosing repository's own log shows it.
open-question.alternative: The check passes whenever the workspace root is inside any git work tree. That covers a subdirectory of a larger repository and a freshly initialized repository with no commits yet. A single probe such as `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` decides it, and no commit is required to exist. The check asks for exactly what the shared commit procedure needs and nothing more. That procedure's path-scoped `git status --porcelain -- <PATHS>`, `git add` and `git commit` all work from a subdirectory and on an unborn HEAD, where the bootstrap commit simply becomes the root commit. Monorepo subprojects are served, and a plain "git init, then re-run" remedy is enough to pass. If the workspace root happens to sit inside an enclosing repository the user never meant to use (for example a home directory tracked as a dotfiles repository), the check passes silently. The bootstrap commit, and every later skill's commit, then lands in that outer repository with no warning.

The check passes only when the repository's top level (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`) is the workspace root itself. A freshly initialized repository with no commits still passes. A workspace root that is only a subdirectory of a larger work tree stops before any write, like the Python check. It rules out committing into an accidental enclosing repository. Every Cairn commit then goes to a repository rooted exactly where `milestones/` and `CLAUDE.md` live, which matches the workflow's assumption that everything is anchored at the workspace root. It refuses monorepo subprojects that the commit procedure would handle correctly. The obvious remedy for such a project, running `git init` in the subdirectory, creates a nested repository, which is worse than the case it guards against. Comparing the two paths also has to cope with symlinked or aliased paths (such as `/var` versus `/private/var` on macOS), or it can fail a root that is really correct.

The check passes inside any git work tree, including a subdirectory, but only once HEAD resolves to at least one commit. A freshly initialized repository with no commits stops, with a remedy asking for an initial commit first. The bootstrap commit never becomes the project's root commit, so the repository's history starts with the user's own content rather than with Cairn scaffolding. The commit procedure never needs this, so the check is stricter than any requirement it enforces. It also makes "git init, then re-run" insufficient on its own: whether that is acceptable depends on how the remedy wording is settled. Either way, the user gets an extra manual step before a brand-new project can be bootstrapped.

alternative.id: Any work tree, advise when nested

open-question.alternative: The check passes inside any git work tree, including one with no commits yet. When the repository's top level differs from the workspace root, the bootstrap still proceeds but also prints an advisory naming the enclosing top level. Monorepo subprojects and fresh repositories are served as in the permissive option. The one case that risks committing into an unintended enclosing repository is still made visible to the user, without refusing it. The advisory does not block, so the scaffolding commit has already landed in the enclosing repository by the time the user reads it. It also adds an output line beyond the single fixed status line the committing skills print. Whether that extra line is allowed depends on how the bootstrap's reporting shape is settled.
